title: Study Abroad Report: Medical University of Vienna
paragraphs: I studied abroad for three months at the Medical University of Vienna in Austria. I decided on the Medical University of Vienna because I was interested in family medicine, because the departments I wished for were easy to get, and because I wanted to see various countries in Europe. For my clerkships, I rotated for one month each through pediatrics (neuro-oncology and NICU, two weeks each), family medicine and emergency medicine.

I did my clerkship in pediatrics for the first month. Pediatrics at the Medical University of Vienna is divided into subspecialties, with a separate large ward and a children's hospital nearby. I did my clerkship in pediatric neuro-oncology for the first two weeks and in the NICU for the remaining two weeks. In neuro-oncology, I was allowed to take histories when the patients or families spoke English, and in the NICU my daily routine was helping with procedures and attending conferences. In both departments, many patients came to the Medical University of Vienna from Eastern European countries in particular, and I was surprised that the doctors and allied health staff talked with patients' families switching between several languages.

In May I rotated through General Practice (family medicine and public health). With doctors from Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan, I visited and listened to talks at various facilities in Vienna. At the end of the month, I left Vienna and did my clerkship as a homestay with a family doctor who practises in a village in the mountains. I visited many places, such as an HIV prevention center, a talk by a school doctor and facilities for homeless people, and learned about healthcare in Austria and other countries. I also felt that I need to become able to explain more about Japan. Being able to talk with doctors from other countries was also a valuable experience.

For the last month I did my clerkship in emergency medicine. The students' work here was securing intravenous lines, ECGs and so on. I had rarely done IV access in clerkships in Japan, and at first it did not go well and I was sorry to have caused patients pain. But the patients in Vienna spoke to me very warmly, and with the help of patients and local students I think I improved little by little in the technique. The local students were truly excellent and did their clerkships like Japanese residents. At the Medical University of Vienna a strong sense of initiative is demanded, and I felt that perhaps it is because they are students who have learned in such an environment that they are excellent, which tightened my resolve to work harder myself.

Outside the clerkships, I was blessed with truly many wonderful encounters: students, Japanese doctors working in Vienna, international students from other countries studying at other universities, members of the volleyball team, my homestay host mother, and people I met at hostels while traveling. Among the many memories, what left the strongest impression on me was the volunteering I did once a week at Ronald McDonald House Vienna (Ronald McDonald House is a lodging facility for sick children and their families). I had originally been volunteering at Nagoya House next to Nagoya University Hospital, and I was interested in the house in Vienna, so I was accepted as a short-term volunteer. At first I did not know the work and could not speak much German, and I flustered around and caused trouble, but the manager, the other volunteers and the families staying there treated me warmly, the children gave me energy, I gradually got used to the work, and each time I talked with many people and had a heartwarming experience. I strongly felt that even when we did not share a language, hearts can connect and we can smile together, and it was a very happy experience from which I learned a lot. Through meeting many people, I felt how interesting it is to talk with people from various backgrounds, and at the same time it was an opportunity to look again at Japan and at myself. Traveling to various countries other than Austria and directly experiencing many cultures and atmospheres was also a truly good experience.

Over the three months there were many times I worried, but including those, I was able to spend a very fulfilling three months and I think I have grown a little. I had the chance to meet people from various countries, and people from every country were wonderful, warm and fun, and I felt really glad that I applied to study abroad. I would like to recommend this program to my juniors. I thank the professors of the International Collaboration Office and the Student Affairs staff who gave me this valuable opportunity, the professors of the Medical University of Vienna, my friends, my family, and everyone who supported me. Thank you very much.
